title: Hypothesis Testing Workflow
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: Step through the flowchart of a hypothesis test with a coin-flip example, set the number of heads and the significance level, and see which decision the p-value leads to.

learningObjectives: Students will be able to apply the steps of a hypothesis test to coin-flip data and decide whether to reject the null hypothesis by comparing the p-value with the significance level.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Step-through of a worked example with adjustable data and immediate feedback on the decision
keyQuestions: What does a p-value of 0.0569 tell you, and what does it not tell you?
Why must α be chosen before looking at the data?
What is the difference between failing to reject H₀ and showing that H₀ is true?
commonMisconceptions: The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true (it is the probability of data at least this extreme, calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true).
Failing to reject H₀ proves H₀ (it only means the evidence against it was not strong enough).
A statistically significant result is an important one (significance says nothing about the size of the effect).
α = 0.05 is a fixed rule (it is a convention, and the same data can lead to different decisions at different levels).
assessmentOpportunities: Students are told that a coin landed heads 38 times in 100 flips, with a two-sided p-value of 0.021. They state H₀ and H₁, make the decision at α = 0.05 and at α = 0.01, and write one sentence that interprets the p-value correctly.
